articles.full_text:
Isometric Approves Five Insurers for Reforestation Carbon Credit Protection
- Insurance framework: Isometric will allow eligible reforestation projects to replace part of their carbon-credit buffer contributions with insurance.
- Five approved providers: Artio, CarbonPool, CFC, Kita and Oka can offer coverage to projects certified by Isometric.
- Project revenue: Developers could retain more carbon removal certificates for sale while maintaining protection against carbon reversals.
Carbon removal registry Isometric has launched an insurance framework with broker Marsh to improve the financial flexibility of certified reforestation projects. The framework allows developers to replace part of their buffer pool contributions with approved insurance policies. Five insurance providers have received approval to participate.
Buffer pools reserve carbon removal certificates against reversals, which occur when stored carbon returns to the atmosphere. Wildfires and disease are among the risks covered by these safeguards. Under Isometric’s new arrangement, eligible developers could retain more certificates for sale, particularly during a project’s early years.
Artio, CarbonPool, CFC, Kita and Oka are the five approved insurance providers. Each can offer coverage to reforestation projects certified by Isometric. Other insurers may apply to join the framework as the registry expands participation.
Isometric said its requirements integrate insurance with existing buffer mechanisms rather than removing reversal protection. The framework aims to ensure each certificate retired by a buyer still represents one tonne of carbon dioxide (CO2) removed. However, Isometric did not disclose insurance pricing, coverage limits, eligibility thresholds or an implementation date.
Bruno Figueiredo, Vice President of Finance at reforestation developer Mombak, described the framework as “an important step toward a more mature carbon market.” He said insurance could improve certainty for buyers and strengthen how projects manage reversal risks.
RELATED ARTICLE: Isometric Expands Carbon Removal Certification to China
Meanwhile, Hema Mistry, Chief Executive of FINPRO UK at Marsh Risk, said “integrating insurance into market infrastructure could help developers expand projects. She also identified greater confidence among buyers, lenders and investors as a potential benefit.”
Isometric is considering extending the framework beyond reforestation to other carbon removal pathways. Developers interested in participating can contact the registry for further information about its requirements. The registry has not identified which additional removal pathways it may include.
Why It Matters
Isometric gains an insurance-backed option within its certification framework, while Marsh extends its role in carbon removal risk management. For developers certified by Isometric, the arrangement could increase the share of certificates available for sale. If insurance costs justify reduced buffer contributions, developers could generate more early-stage certificate revenue to support project expansion.

articles.summary: Commission Data Show EU Green Bond Issuance Reaches €39 Billion in 2026  ESG News
articles.full_text:
- Taxonomy investment: Over €320 billion was invested in EU Taxonomy-aligned activities in 2025.
- Cumulative investment: Over €1.2 trillion has been invested in sustainable activities since 2021.
- Green bond issuance: Around €60 billion has been issued since December 2024.
The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, says over €1.2 trillion has been invested in sustainable activities since 2021. According to the figures, over €320 billion was invested in 2025 in activities aligned with the EU Taxonomy. The Taxonomy is the classification system that helps companies and investors identify environmentally sustainable activities. Meanwhile, the energy sector accounted for the largest share, driven mainly by electricity providers, according to the Commission.
The Commission says the figures also show continued growth in use of the EU’s sustainable finance framework. The framework links economic growth with decarbonisation by supporting the roll-out of clean technologies and infrastructure, especially in the energy sector. By channeling investment into domestic renewable energy, electrification and other clean technologies, the framework reduces reliance on imported fossil fuels, the Commission says. Notably, the release did not describe the methodology used to calculate the investment and issuance figures.
European Green Bonds are also gaining momentum, with around €60 billion issued since December 2024. That total includes €21 billion in 2025 and a further €39 billion from 1 January to 7 October 2026. The Commission says the 2026 amount is nearly double the amount issued in the first year, pointing to growing use of the standard. The European Green Bond Standard is a voluntary framework for bonds that finance Taxonomy-aligned activities.

Who It Affects
- Bond issuers: The European Green Bond Standard is voluntary and applies to bonds that finance Taxonomy-aligned activities.
- Electricity providers: They mainly drove the energy sector’s large share of 2025 Taxonomy-aligned investment, the largest of any sector.
- Companies and investors: The Commission is simplifying the sustainable finance framework to make it easier to implement.

articles.title: Biodiversity, Guterres: “The war on nature is far from over” - Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
articles.summary: Biodiversity, Guterres: “The war on nature is far from over”  Materia Rinnovabile | Renewable Matter
articles.full_text:
Fewer than half of national biodiversity targets are on track. This is the most significant finding in the report State of Biodiversity Action, presented on 15 October in Yerevan by United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres. This document is crucial for guiding the biodiversity negotiations at COP17, which began on Monday 19 October and will run until 30 October in the Armenian capital, Yerevan.
The State of Biodiversity Action is the first global assessment of progress on the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in December 2022 with twenty-three targets for 2030 and four milestones for 2050. It is the cornerstone strategy for biodiversity protection, effectively nature’s Paris Agreement: nearly two hundred countries signed it four years ago.
“It’s not all bad news; there is also some positive news in the report,” Guterres told journalists covering the press conference. “For example, there has been a great deal of progress, even if it is not enough.” It will now be up to the participants in the COP17 negotiations to raise the level of ambition.
Many commitments, few results
Halfway through the process, formal participation is widespread. Almost 90% of the 196 Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have set national targets, around 60% have updated strategies and action plans, and over 70% have submitted national reports. Indigenous peoples, local communities, sub-national governments, businesses and civil society have registered around 5,000 grassroots commitments to actions aimed at protecting and restoring nature.
But commitment has not been followed by implementation. National targets cover, on average, 22 of the 23 global targets, but often only partially. Many countries promise positive incentives, but few are committed to reducing harmful subsidies, as called for by Target 18: the commitment is to cut them by $500 billion a year by 2030, and progress has been slow. Target 3, known as 30by30 – the protection of 30% of land and seas by 2030 – also remains a long way off.
Then there is the issue of financial resources. The State of Biodiversity Action report notes that developed countries are failing to bridge the “biodiversity finance gap” of $200 billion.
Initiatives aimed at supporting this objective are facing difficulties: a special “framework” fund for biodiversity has received less than $140 million from developed countries over the past two years, while the “long-standing” Cali Fund on DSI (on the use of digital sequences relating to genetic resources) has raised just $6,000 from private companies. Private individuals are the ones trying to bridge the gap. The Species Recovery Donor Alliance, composed of nine donors, including the Bezos Earth Fund set up by the founder of Amazon, has pledged to invest $500 million by 2030 to support the recovery of endangered species in over one hundred countries, as announced by Cristian Samper, managing director and head of Nature Solutions at the Bezos Earth Fund, at the Leaders’ Summit held on the sidelines of COP17. The availability of funding – or the lack thereof – will be one of the main points of contention in the COP17 negotiations.
Among the financial priorities, the report highlights the reform of harmful incentives, sustainable production and consumption, more rigorous corporate reporting on their impacts and their dependence on nature, and investment directed towards conservation and restoration. According to UN data, for every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, around 30 end up in activities that degrade it. “The report shows that many of the elements critical to progress, including finance, capacity, cooperation and data, are still missing,” said Guterres. “Nature will not thrive good intentions alone.”
At a press conference, the Secretary-General was even more direct. “The key issue is [political and economic] influence.” That of the mining industry, certainly, but also agribusiness, which destroys forests, and intensive fishing – sectors that still have “too much influence to preserve their economic power” and use it to sway policy. The way forward, according to Guterres, lies with the market: “We must change the balance of power.”
“COP15 gave us the legal framework,” said Hambardzum Matevosyan, Armenia’s Minister for the Environment and incoming President of COP17. “COP16 advanced important mechanisms for its implementation. COP17 must now help us determine where we stand, what is working, where progress is falling short, and what must change.” According to Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP, “we cannot tackle climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution in isolation”. Another proposal on the table is the Yerevan Pathway – a roadmap still under negotiation – aimed at accelerating progress towards the targets of the Montreal-Kunming Agreement.
No major technical negotiations are expected at the talks; rather, the focus is on tangible commitments from individual countries, ranging from nature conservation to the mobilisation of financial resources. “We know how far we have come,” concluded Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary of the Convention. “We know where the gaps lie. Now we must work together to fill them.”

articles.title: Africans reuse, repair, recycle and resell waste: what’s needed to build on the circular economy basics - The Conversation
articles.summary: Africans reuse, repair, recycle and resell waste: what’s needed to build on the circular economy basics  The Conversation
articles.full_text:
In many African cities, a broken fridge is rarely thrown away immediately. It may be repaired and resold, dismantled for spare parts or collected for its metal components.
Old clothes are often altered or transformed into something new. Leftover crop stalks and leaves are turned into animal feed, compost, cooking fuel or biogas.
These activities are often driven by need. Incomes are limited and it’s expensive to replace appliances or worn out clothes. Sometimes recycling also happens because of unreliable waste collection.
Read more: Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa: how they stack up on reusing waste
These are also examples of a circular economy. This is where products and materials are kept in use for as long as possible. It’s the opposite of a system where resources are extracted from nature and turned into goods that are sold, used and eventually thrown away.
We are circular economy specialists who look at how recycling and repair practices are already part of everyday economic activity across Africa. Our aim is to find ways for policymakers to take small projects and scale them up.
In our latest research, we looked at policies and examples from African countries to find out how circular economy practices are taking off on the continent.
Our research found that circular economies aren’t happening everywhere. Thirty-four African countries have banned plastic bags to some degree. Rwanda, Ethiopia, Ghana, Nigeria, South Africa and Morocco have set up facilities to recycle e-waste (discarded electronic devices). They’ve also set up projects that turn waste into energy. Kenya has rules that make manufacturers responsible for collecting and recycling their products after people finish using them.
Somalia, Sudan and Congo, however, still depend heavily on a system in which products are made, used and discarded.
Africa’s circular economy has been discussed by governments, businesses, development agencies and international organisations as if it needs to be based on an imported model of formal waste-management systems and high-tech recycling.
Read more: West Africa’s plastic waste could be fuelling the economy instead of polluting the ocean: experts
These approaches may have a role, but repairers, reclaimers (also known as waste pickers), farmers and small businesses across Africa are already repairing, reusing, reselling, sharing, recovering materials and converting organic waste into productive resources.
In other words, circular practices are already embedded in everyday economic activity in African countries. The priority is therefore not to replace these practices. What’s needed is to recognise and improve them, and find ways to make them happen on a bigger scale. This means giving local businesses and communities the finance, infrastructure, skills and supportive policies they need to expand what is already working.
Progress is possible but uneven
Our research found that several African countries have introduced policies and initiatives supporting aspects of a circular economy. For example, Rwanda has acted against plastic pollution and developed facilities for processing electronic waste.
South Africa has come up with rules for producers of goods to help manage and pay for their products even after selling them. These rules compel producers to support collection, reuse and recycling. This keeps materials in circulation and reduces waste.
Read more: Ghana’s businesses don’t always need costly tech. How to build on what’s already been done
Kenya has taken significant measures against single use plastic bags. In Ghana, the National Plastic Action Partnership brings together government, business and civil society. Nigeria is developing a national circular economy roadmap. Nigerian groups like Wecyclers have connected informal collectors with recycling markets.
Greater opportunities exist across agriculture and food systems, manufacturing, energy, and water and sanitation.
However, a policy on paper does not automatically produce an effective system. Waste collection remains inadequate in many African cities. There aren’t many recycling facilities on the continent. Local authorities often lack the funds, equipment and technical capacity to enforce regulations. Political instability and unreliable electricity supplies can make long term investment in circular economy projects difficult.
What needs to happen next
Africa’s move towards a circular economy must start with the basics: collecting waste, sorting it properly and disposing of it safely. As our research found, expensive technologies will not work well if waste is never collected or is too contaminated to recycle.
The African Union’s Continental Circular Economy Action Plan has some useful ideas on this. But its success will depend on how well it is put into practice in local communities. For many countries, improving everyday waste services should come before investing in high-tech solutions.
Read more: How the plastics industry shifted responsibility for recycling onto you, the consumer
Informal workers including reclaimers, repairers and second-hand traders are already central to Africa’s circular economy. They should be supported by governments. They need training, safer working conditions, facilities to work in, fair compensation and social protection. Including these workers in formal circular economy systems, while protecting their livelihoods, can help build a more inclusive and effective circular economy.
The success of circular economy policies should be judged on more than how much waste is kept out of rubbish dumps. Policymakers need to make sure that people benefit from the circular economy. Working conditions of recyclers should improve, recovered products must be affordable and local recycling enterprises must remain viable.
Read more: The circular economy may not be taking off: Here are six ways stakeholders can make it happen
Africa’s circular economy will emerge strongly if governments, businesses, communities, researchers and informal workers work together. The foundations of a circular economy already exist. African countries have a strong culture of repairing and reusing goods. Local experts and entrepreneurs who turn discarded materials into value are valued. The task now is to support these efforts without destroying the social and economic systems that sustain them.

articles.title: Việt Nam releases forest map as a data foundation to support EUDR compliance - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: Việt Nam releases forest map as a data foundation to support EUDR compliance  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| A forest in Lào Cai Province. — VNA/VNS Photo | 
HÀ NỘI — The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development’s Department of Forestry on Tuesday unveiled the 2020 Forest Boundary Map, Version 1.0 (VFM2020.v1), with an aim to help businesses meet the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).
The map provides reference data to help businesses in the timber, coffee and rubber sectors assess their sourcing areas, ensure traceability and compile evidence for compliance with the EUDR.
This foundational dataset serves as a resource for regulatory authorities, local governments and businesses to verify and cross-reference information regarding the status of forests, thereby enhancing transparency within the supply chains of exported commodities.
Speaking at the launch, Nguyễn Văn Diện, deputy director of the department, said that the EUDR imposes rigorous requirements concerning legality, traceability and the provision of evidence to prove that products are not linked to deforestation or forest degradation occurring after December 31, 2020.
Meeting these requirements presents both a challenge and an impetus for Việt Nam to innovate its management practices, accelerate the digital transformation of forest resource data, and bolster the reputation of its products in the international market.
In this context, the map has been developed to provide a unified source of spatial information nationwide, enabling businesses to pinpoint their sourcing areas and cross-reference them against forest data as of 2020. The map is integrated into a WebGIS platform and accessible at eudr.vnforest.gov.vn, facilitating easy lookup and data retrieval.
However, Diện noted that the map serves only as a reference document for verification and cross-checking purposes. It is not the sole basis for determining whether a product complies with the EUDR. Businesses are still required to fully meet all regulatory requirements and provide traceability documentation along with relevant supporting evidence.
According to Phạm Văn Duẩn, deputy director of the Institute of Forest Ecology and Environment, the map was developed in a context where businesses must rely on various map sources to verify information for EUDR compliance. Establishing a unified reference dataset provides stakeholders with an additional basis for identifying areas that require further verification.
The map was developed by integrating 2020 forest data provided by local authorities, remote sensing imagery, international reference maps and the findings of local-level reviews. Areas where discrepancies emerged between different data sources were flagged for verification against forest management records and on-the-ground information.
The development process comprised six key stages: standardising 2020 forest data, reviewing maps of the three designated forest categories, assessing the reliability of various information sources, analysing changes via remote sensing imagery, conducting local-level validation and finalising the database within a WebGIS system.
A notable point discussed during the launch was the comparison between the VFM2020.v1 dataset and the GFC2020 (version 4) map, developed by the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC).
According to Phạm Ngọc Hải from the Forest Inventory and Planning Institute under the Vietnamese Academy of Forest Sciences, comparing these two data sources aims to assess their level of alignment, identify areas of discrepancy and propose improvements to the maps to support the implementation of the EUDR.
The comparison, conducted within forest land areas covered by the VFM2020.v1 dataset, reveals a 78.5 per cent consensus between the two maps, and a 21.5 per cent rate of discrepancy. Specifically, for natural forests, the level of agreement reaches 92 per cent.
However, approximately 1.73 million hectares classified as forest in the VFM2020.v1 dataset are not categorised as forest in the JRC map. Conversely, about 2.25 million hectares identified as forest by the JRC are classified as non-forest in the VFM2020 dataset.
According to Phạm Ngọc Hải, these discrepancies may stem from differences in the objectives, scope and classification methodologies used for each map. For instance, certain areas under rubber or coffee cultivation might be categorised as ‘forest’ in VFM2020, whereas the JRC does not classify them as such. Conversely, areas containing shrubs or regenerating vegetation might be identified as forest by the JRC, but are not classified that way in Việt Nam’s dataset.
The comparison results also help identify priority areas for refinement, such as reviewing commercial crop areas currently labeled as forest, updating changes that have not yet been fully captured and re-examining the classification of natural versus planted forests in areas where discrepancies exist.
The Department of Forestry and the Forest Protection Department noted that the release of VFM2020.v1 does not mark the end of the mapping process. Rather, it serves as a starting point for ongoing verification, updating and quality improvement, based on empirical evidence and feedback from specialised agencies, local authorities and businesses.
The Department of Forestry and the Forest Protection Department will collaborate with scientists, specialised agencies and local authorities to review and address remaining discrepancies through a standardised procedure. — BIZHUB/VNS

articles.title: Fragmented waste taxes distorting Europe’s circular economy, new report warns - Circular Online
articles.summary: Fragmented waste taxes distorting Europe’s circular economy, new report warns  Circular Online
articles.full_text:
Europe’s fragmented waste taxes risk undermining efforts to reduce landfill, strengthen recycling, and improve energy security, a new report warns.
The 38-country analysis from the RDF Industry Group (RDFIG) calls for a more coherent European approach to residual waste taxation as the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) expands.
The RDFIG wants European and national policymakers to align landfill and Energy from Waste (EfW) taxation to ensure treatment decisions are made based on capacity, efficiency and environmental performance, rather than differences in national tax burdens.
The Uneven Playing Field: How Europe’s Waste Taxes Distort Recovery, Landfill and Trade report maps landfill taxes and restrictions alongside incineration taxes across 38 European countries.
The 2026 analysis identifies landfill taxes in 63% of countries (24 out of 38), with rates ranging from approximately €11 to €154 per tonne.
Incineration taxation is identified in 34% (13 out of 38), with combined tax burdens ranging from €8 to approximately €98 per tonne.
The report argues that the differences in tax rates contribute to comparable recovery facilities being more or less competitive based on their location.
It also warned that additional taxation of recovery without sufficient landfill deterrence risks pushing fiscal incentives against the waste hierarchy.
Robert Corijn, Chair of the RDF Industry Group’s Policy Working Group, commented: “Europe wants to reduce landfill, recover resources and strengthen its energy security. Those ambitions depend on making better use of the infrastructure we already have, across national borders.”
“Waste should move because a facility offers suitable capacity, efficient energy recovery or access to decarbonisation infrastructure. National tax differences should not determine which facilities can compete.”
The report calls for recovery capacity to be considered collectively across Europe, rather than assuming every country must build sufficient facilities to treat all its own residual waste.
It argues that cross-border recovery can connect countries with limited treatment options to existing capacity elsewhere, including facilities supplying district heat or developing carbon capture and storage.
The implications also extend beyond EfW, the report warns. It says that higher taxes on sorting and recycling processes that produce residues increase the cost of producing recycled materials, potentially weakening their competitiveness against virgin alternatives.
The report found that, without wider reform, ETS could leave landfill taxed more leniently than incineration in more than 10 countries, with the tax differential narrowing towards parity in others.
It concludes that the risk is greatest where higher carbon costs on EfW coincide with substantial landfill availability and weak fiscal or regulatory restrictions.
Commenting on the report, Andy Jones, Chair of the RDF Industry Group, said: “Europe has spent decades building a waste hierarchy designed to deliver better environmental outcomes.”
“As carbon pricing expands and fiscal frameworks evolve, we must ensure that taxation supports that hierarchy rather than undermines it.”

PepsiCo Signs Five Startup Agreements to Explore Sustainability Technology Deployment Across Asia Pacific
- Five agreements signed: PepsiCo signed letters of intent with Adiona, Bali Waste Cycle, Beijing AIForce Tech, Takachar and X-Centric Sciences.
- Commercial readiness: The seven-month accelerator assessed technical, operational and commercial requirements for potential deployment across Asia Pacific.
- Program track record: Since 2023, PepsiCo’s regional Greenhouse Program has worked with 30 startups and supported 22 pilots.
PepsiCo has signed five letters of intent with sustainability startups following its seven-month Greenhouse Program APAC 2026: The IMPACT Edition. The agreements cover potential commercial applications in agricultural technology, packaging recovery, logistics efficiency, soil intelligence and biochar across Asia Pacific.
The program brought five returning alumni together with PepsiCo teams from sustainability, procurement, research and development, operations, finance and legal. Each startup assessed how its technology could meet business requirements and progress toward commercial deployment.
Adiona signed an agreement to explore logistics network optimisation in China, building on earlier work involving AI-powered route planning. Beijing AIForce Tech will explore further agricultural technology collaboration in China, where its 140HP electric tractor already operates under a five-year commercial lease. Its larger 180HP model is undergoing testing scheduled to finish by the end of 2026.
Bali Waste Cycle will examine expanded flexible packaging recovery and recycling applications in Indonesia. Takachar will evaluate potential uses for its portable agricultural residue-to-biochar technology across Asia Pacific. Meanwhile, X-Centric Sciences will explore precision soil intelligence applications following agricultural field trials in Australia.
RELATED ARTICLE: PepsiCo Doubles Regenerative Farming Footprint to Over 1.8 Million Acres: 2023 PepsiCo ESG Report
PepsiCo said future deployment remains subject to performance assessments, operational fit, business value and further agreement. The company did not disclose financial terms, deployment volumes or commercial launch dates for the five agreements.
“Building resilient, growing businesses in Asia Pacific will increasingly require collaboration across sectors and capabilities,” said Anne Tse, Chief Executive Officer, Asia Pacific, PepsiCo. “Through the Greenhouse Accelerator, we are bringing entrepreneurs together with PepsiCo teams to test emerging solutions against real business and operational challenges across the food system. The opportunity goes beyond any single technology or partnership. By working with startups, investors, and other partners, we can help create stronger connections across the innovation ecosystem, explore solutions with the potential to support business resilience and growth.”
Greenhouse Program Track Record
Since launching in Asia Pacific in 2023, PepsiCo’s Greenhouse Program has supported 22 pilots involving 30 startups across four editions. The 2026 edition placed greater emphasis on commercial readiness, building on its earlier grant-based accelerator model.
Separately, Beijing AIForce Tech reported a US$60 million Series B funding round. X-Centric Sciences was also selected for Google DeepMind’s first AI for the Planet accelerator in Asia Pacific.
Why It Matters
PepsiCo gains five potential technology partnerships that could support its pep+ sustainability strategy across agriculture, logistics and packaging. The startups gain access to PepsiCo’s operational teams and evaluation processes across regional markets. If further assessments and commercial agreements succeed, the partnerships could lead to expanded technology deployment within PepsiCo’s Asia Pacific supply chain.

articles.title: Citi Closes $72 Million Carbon Removal-Linked Note for Texas Biochar Project
articles.summary:
Citi has closed a $72 million, 3.5-year principal-protected Carbon Removal-Linked Note to finance Applied Carbon’s biochar project in Texas. The structure links investor payments to verified carbon removals rather than […]
The post Citi Closes $72 Million Carbon Removal-Linked Note for Texas Biochar Project appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Citi Closes $72 Million Carbon Removal-Linked Note for Texas Biochar Project
- $72 Million Financing: Citi closed a 3.5-year principal-protected note to fund Applied Carbon’s biochar project in Texas.
- Credit-Linked Returns: Investors receive payments tied to verified carbon credit issuance and delivery instead of traditional coupons.
- Microsoft Offtake: A 2022 agreement provides long-term demand for a portion of Applied Carbon’s carbon removal credits.
Citi has closed a $72 million, 3.5-year principal-protected Carbon Removal-Linked Note to finance Applied Carbon’s biochar project in Texas. The structure links investor payments to verified carbon removals rather than traditional bond coupons. Citi describes it as its first outcome bond tied to verified carbon removals.
The financing directs upfront capital toward Applied Carbon’s operations. Investors forego conventional coupon payments and instead receive payments linked to carbon credits issued and delivered by the project. The arrangement connects project financing with measurable carbon removal outcomes.
Applied Carbon uses mobile pyrolysis technology to convert agricultural crop residue into biochar, a stable, carbon-rich material that stores carbon in soil. Its equipment processes residue directly in agricultural fields, combining production and application in one pass. The platform also operates at field edges, allowing greater flexibility in sourcing agricultural waste.
Citi said the structure builds on its previous work connecting bond performance with environmental outcomes. “The voluntary carbon market requires new financial structures to bridge the gap between investor capital and the long-term funding needs of carbon removal projects,” said Sonia Battikh, Global Head of Carbon Offsets Trading at Citi. “This Carbon Removal-Linked Note builds on Citi’s pioneering work linking bond performance to environmental outcomes and marks our first outcome bond tied to verified carbon removals. By bringing together investors, project developers and long-term carbon demand, we are continuing to expand the range of opportunities through which capital markets can finance real-world outcomes.”
Applied Carbon plans to scale deployments across Texas with Citi and Nuveen. “This financing shows that biochar and engineered carbon removal projects can be structured and financed like any other asset,” said Jason Aramburu, Founder & CEO at Applied Carbon. “We’re proud to work with Citi and Nuveen to scale our deployments and deliver real impact for the climate and for farmers across Texas. This is the kind of structure that will unlock capital for carbon removal at scale”.
Nuveen participated in the financing, citing the project’s valuation, impact reporting and potential carbon credit generation. “We are excited to have participated in Citigroup’s inaugural outcome bond given its attractive relative valuation, unique underlying project and commitment to robust impact reporting,” said Stephen M. Liberatore, CFA, Head of ESG/Impact for Global Fixed Income at Nuveen. “The funding of equipment to produce biochar from agricultural waste through in-field processing is an excellent fit for our portfolios. These are the types of investments that we expect will produce not only direct and measurable impact through high-permanence carbon sequestration but also improve sustainable free cash flow generation through the creation of carbon credits that are being off-taken by a well-known hyperscaler.”
Microsoft signed an offtake agreement with Applied Carbon in 2022 covering a portion of the project’s carbon credits. That commitment provides long-term demand for the underlying removal activity. Citi did not disclose the expected credit volume, investor payment formula or deployment schedule.
RELATED ARTICLE: Citi and IFC Announce $2 billion Sustainable Supply Chain Finance Program Focused on Emerging Markets
Why It Matters
For Citi, the note adds verified carbon removals to its outcome-linked financing structures. Applied Carbon gains upfront financing for equipment deployments, supported by Microsoft’s existing carbon credit purchase commitment. Nuveen gains exposure to a principal-protected investment tied to measurable carbon removal. articles.full_text:
Canada’s Sustainable Finance Taxonomy Defines Green and Transition Investment Criteria
- Core categories confirmed: Canada’s final taxonomy methodology defines green and transition investments, with further research planned on an abatement measures category.
- Sector criteria underway: Technical screening criteria for six priority sectors are scheduled for completion by the end of 2027.
- Stakeholder input: The methodology incorporates 70 expert advisors, nearly 200 public submissions and perspectives from over 30 Indigenous organizations.
Canada’s Taxonomy and Transition Planning Council has released its final Methodology Report, establishing the framework for the Canadian Sustainable Finance Taxonomy. Published on October 20, 2026, the report confirms green and transition investment categories, environmental and social safeguards, and core principles. The voluntary framework aims to give investors consistent criteria for identifying climate-aligned economic activities across Canada.
The methodology incorporates international practices while accounting for Canada’s economic structure, geography, legal framework and Indigenous Rights. It also sets out decisions requiring further research before the taxonomy’s technical criteria are finalized.
The Council determined that insufficient information exists to include or exclude a separate abatement measures category. Further feasibility research will assess whether such activities align with the taxonomy’s objectives, ambition and principles. Meanwhile, proposed environmental and social safeguards, including protections concerning Indigenous Rights, will undergo consultation during the next development stage.
The final methodology draws on global evidence, input from 70 expert advisors and nearly 200 public feedback submissions. Representatives of more than 30 Indigenous organizations also contributed perspectives to the process.
Marlene Puffer, Chair of the Canadian Taxonomy and Transition Planning Council, emphasized the remaining work and the framework’s investment objectives. “While we still have a lot of work ahead of us, the Methodology Report marks a significant milestone for sustainable finance in Canada. This strong foundation sets us on course to deliver the credible, usable, interoperable taxonomy that investors need to confidently invest in Canada’s needs and opportunities, aligned with the path to net zero by mid-century.”

Sector Criteria and Implementation
The Canadian Climate Institute, the taxonomy’s research custodian, has established technical working groups for electricity, buildings and transportation. Criteria for these sectors, alongside mining, manufacturing and forestry/agriculture, are scheduled for development by the end of 2027.
The criteria will define qualifying near-zero activities, identify dead-end transition pathways and assess potential inclusion of nuclear energy, data centres and carbon removals. Business Future Pathways plans to publish draft sectoral criteria for public feedback later this winter. The Council has not specified a final adoption date or enforcement arrangements.
Who It Affects
- Investors and financial institutions: Will gain defined green and transition categories for assessing climate-aligned investments.
- Companies across six sectors: Will receive activity-specific screening criteria and guardrails as the taxonomy develops.
- Indigenous rights holders: Will have further opportunities to comment on proposed safeguards addressing Indigenous Rights.

articles.full_text:
84% of Asset Owners Now Use Sustainability in Investing, FTSE Russell Survey Finds
- Adoption rebound: 84% of asset owners now factor in sustainability, up from 73% in 2025.
- Governance priority: Governance, tax and shareholder rights top the list at 32%, up from 18%.
- Reporting barrier: Corporate reporting and disclosure quality is the leading barrier to adoption.
FTSE Russell, LSEG’s global index provider, reports that 84% of asset owners now factor sustainability into investment decisions, up from 73% in 2025. The ninth annual survey covered 402 asset owners across 24 countries, and another 15% are evaluating adoption. Eighty-five percent expect to do more over the next one to three years, and none expect to do less. The summary did not disclose the survey period or response rate.
More than half of respondents (51%) now apply sustainability to over 50% of their assets, up from 26% last year. Eleven percent apply it to their whole portfolio, up from 0% in 2025, and 47% invest sustainably to improve returns, up from 41%.
Sustainability is “becoming a broader part of mainstream investment processes,” said Lee Clements, Head of Applied Sustainable Investment Research at FTSE Russell, who added that investors are “seeing more tangible examples of sustainability considerations [such as] extreme heat events over the summer or the impact of the current energy shock on driving the energy transition.”
Governance, tax and shareholder rights is now the top sustainability priority, cited by 32% of respondents, up from 18% in 2025. Asset owners also flagged health and healthcare risks (25%), technology and AI issues (24%) and food security (19%).
Clements tied the governance concerns to “pressure on shareholder rights” and “potential regulatory proposals which could limit disclosure and the ability of investors to bring items to vote,” and added that “geopolitical and macro[economic] volatility and a potential down market could uncover any lurking governance issues in companies.”
How Sentiment Has Shifted
Adoption fell from 86% in 2022 to 71% in 2024, which Clements linked to geopolitical backlash and revised disclosure rules. This year, one-quarter rate climate risk concern 10 out of 10, up from 11%, and 52% weigh it in asset allocation, up from 36%. Thirty percent pursue divestment from high-carbon assets, up from 21%, while 60% still pursue engagement, down from 67%.
Looking ahead, “Stability of government policy and approach on sustainability will have an impact on adoption, as will the overall direction of the market and broader economy,” Clements said, adding that “the biggest question” LSEG receives is how the proliferation of data centers and AI infrastructure “will impact sustainability considerations.”

Who It Affects
- Corporate issuers: Reporting and disclosure quality is the leading barrier, cited by 33% of owners, up from 31%.
- Large AI companies: Asset owners cited governance issues at these firms as a concern, and LSEG noted it in the report.
- Policymakers and regulators: 36% of owners now see regulatory turbulence as a potential enabler of sustainable investment, up from 22%.

Peak Energy, Hyundai Motor Securities Launch Solar JV With Five Supplier Projects
- Five initial projects: The joint venture has secured five rooftop solar projects targeting Hyundai Motor’s Tier-1 automotive suppliers.
- Expansion potential: The initiative could reach 100 MW across hundreds of supplier sites, avoiding approximately 55,000 tons of CO2 annually.
- Cost stability: Long-term solar power purchase agreements aim to reduce electricity price volatility and improve supplier operating margins.
Peak Energy and the Vencore Rooftop Equity Fund, associated with Hyundai Motor Securities, have launched a renewable energy joint venture in South Korea. The venture targets energy-intensive automotive suppliers, with five initial projects secured among major Tier-1 suppliers to Hyundai Motor. It aims to provide competitive electricity pricing through long-term solar power purchase agreements (PPAs).
The partnership combines Peak Energy’s renewable project development capabilities with Hyundai Motor Securities’ financing expertise. It focuses on manufacturers producing key automotive components, whose electricity consumption contributes to Hyundai’s Scope 3 value-chain emissions. The companies aim to reduce supplier exposure to power price volatility while supporting manufacturing competitiveness and decarbonization.
The initial projects establish a foundation for expansion across several hundred supplier sites nationwide. The venture has a long-term potential of 100 MW of industrial rooftop solar capacity. At that scale, the companies estimate annual emissions avoidance of approximately 55,000 tons of CO2. Lifetime avoided emissions could exceed 1 million tons.
The announcement comes as export uncertainty, global trade risks and margin pressure affect automotive suppliers. However, the companies did not disclose the joint venture’s financial terms, project investment amounts or commissioning schedule.
Gavin Adda, CEO of Peak Energy, said the venture connects electricity costs directly with industrial competitiveness. He highlighted Hyundai Motor Securities’ early recognition of this issue and the initial project pipeline. “Industrial competitiveness is now increasingly tied to the price of electricity. Hyundai Motor Securities recognized this early and moved quickly. This joint venture offers Korea’s OEM suppliers a clear path to gaining long-term visibility into power costs through solar PPAs, while advancing the decarbonization of the supply chain. The fact that five projects are already set to be signed shows that this model is moving into concrete execution on the ground. For Peak Energy, this partnership is both a strong vote of confidence from a world-class industrial supply chain and recognition of the track record we’ve built across Korea and Asia.”
A representative from Hyundai Motor Securities’ Infrastructure Investment Division described the partnership as a practical route to renewable electricity adoption. The division expects financing structures and project execution capabilities to support broader deployment.
“This collaboration marks an important first step toward supporting the automotive supply chain’s practical transition to renewable energy. Through our joint venture with Peak Energy, Hyundai Motor Securities plans to combine competitive financing structures with strong project execution capabilities, enabling domestic suppliers to adopt solar PPAs in a reliable and sustainable manner. We will continue to expand the initiative, contributing to carbon emissions reductions across the supply chain and supporting its long-term sustainable growth.”

Existing Renewable Energy Portfolio
Peak Energy currently holds more than 300 MW of operating renewable energy assets across Asia-Pacific. More than 200 MW is operating or expected to operate soon in Korea. Backed by infrastructure investment firm Stonepeak, the company has experience delivering long-term PPA-based industrial renewable energy projects.
Why It Matters
Peak Energy gains a dedicated route into Hyundai’s automotive supplier network, adding five projects to its Korean development pipeline. Hyundai Motor Securities gains a channel to deploy financing structures alongside renewable energy project execution. If the initial projects proceed successfully, the venture could expand solar PPA contracts across hundreds of supplier sites toward its 100 MW potential.

articles.summary:
The euro zone economy has proved more resilient to this year’s energy shock than expected, according to European Central Bank (ECB) economists. Lower fossil fuel dependence, artificial intelligence investment and […]
The post ECB Finds Euro Zone Oil Dependence Halved as AI and Fiscal Spending Support Growth appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
ECB Finds Euro Zone Oil Dependence Halved as AI and Fiscal Spending Support Growth
- Lower oil exposure: The euro zone economy is about half as reliant on oil as in the early 1990s, ECB economists estimate.
- Stronger fiscal support: Fiscal stimulus reached 0.5% of GDP, twice the level expected at the end of last year.
- Temporary growth drivers: ECB economists warn that AI investment, global demand and government spending may fade.
The euro zone economy has proved more resilient to this year’s energy shock than expected, according to European Central Bank (ECB) economists. Lower fossil fuel dependence, artificial intelligence investment and stronger government spending have helped sustain growth despite higher oil and gas prices.
Energy Dependence and Economic Resilience
ECB economists Oscar Arce, Gerrit Koester and Beatrice Pierluigi published the assessment in an ECB blog on Wednesday. They estimated that the euro area now relies on oil about half as much as in the early 1990s. This reduction has limited the economic impact of rising energy prices.
The Iran war disrupted energy markets, pushing oil and gas prices higher and renewing inflation concerns. However, the currency bloc has continued expanding, with business surveys showing that economic activity remains positive. Higher renewable and nuclear electricity generation has also weakened the connection between gas prices and electricity costs in several countries.
AI Investment and Fiscal Support
The ECB economists identified AI-related trade as an “important tailwind” for the euro area. Technology-related export orders and sectors linked to AI have outperformed, supporting economic activity during the energy shock.
Government spending has also exceeded earlier expectations. The fiscal impulse reached 0.5% of gross domestic product, twice the level projected at the end of last year. German government spending on defence and infrastructure accounted for much of the additional support.
However, the economists cautioned that several growth drivers could prove temporary. Global demand, fiscal stimulus and AI investment may weaken, particularly if geopolitical tensions intensify or energy markets face further disruption.
Monetary Policy Implications
The findings arrive as the ECB considers further interest rate increases to contain energy-driven inflation. A third rate increase this year is expected in December, following renewed inflation pressures and a global bond selloff.
The ECB assessment identifies reduced oil exposure as a structural source of resilience, alongside shorter-term support from investment and fiscal policy. However, its economists warn that fresh energy disruptions could leave the euro area vulnerable if those temporary sources of growth weaken.

Who It Affects
- Euro zone businesses: Lower oil dependence and stronger electricity generation diversity have reduced exposure to energy price shocks in several countries.
- Technology exporters: AI-related investment and trade have supported stronger export orders and activity in AI-linked sectors.
- European policymakers: Energy-led inflation and the possibility of fading fiscal support complicate decisions on further interest rate increases.

Amazon Backs Feasibility Work on 960 MW Indiana Nuclear Project
- Project scope: A 12-unit Xe-100 plant with 960 MW of proposed capacity.
- Amazon funding: Amazon provides certain project development funding for the feasibility work.
- Collaboration goal: Second commercial deployment toward more than 5 GW of new U.S. nuclear capacity by 2039.
X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) have announced a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) to advance feasibility work. The work covers a proposed 960 MW Xe-100 small modular reactor (SMR) project in Indiana. Amazon is providing certain project development funding for the effort. The project would also be the second commercial deployment under the collaboration between Amazon and X-energy.
The 12-unit plant would redevelop an AEP-owned brownfield (previously developed) site near the former Breed Generating Station in Sullivan County, Indiana. Together, the proposed project would combine AEP’s power generation and nuclear operating expertise, Amazon’s milestone-based development capital and X-energy’s advanced nuclear technology. The companies did not disclose the project’s cost, construction timeline or power purchaser.
“Advanced nuclear energy has the potential to provide dependable power for over half a century while supporting economic growth in our communities. With this development plan, we are working to bring together the resources to help meet unprecedented growth in energy demand with reliable baseload power while protecting affordability for existing customers. Our agreements with Amazon and X-energy will provide all necessary capital protections and financial safeguards that we have said are essential for any potential nuclear project to move forward,” said Bill Fehrman, Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer of AEP.
The Xe-100 is an 80 MWe (megawatts electric) high-temperature, gas-cooled reactor that uses helium coolant and tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) fuel. The U.S. Department of Energy calls this fuel the “most robust nuclear fuel on earth” because it withstands extreme temperatures without melting. Meanwhile, since 2025, Governor Mike Braun and the Indiana General Assembly have enacted supportive state policies, including investment and manufacturing tax credits.
“Indiana is building an energy future that prioritizes affordability for Hoosier families and businesses while driving economic growth. The decision by I&M/AEP, Amazon and X-energy to explore this technology in one of Indiana’s counties represents the kind of innovation and investment that can deliver lasting benefits for our state. This project has the potential to create well-paying jobs in Sullivan County, strengthen our electric grid and further position Indiana as a national leader in advanced nuclear energy,” said Indiana Governor Mike Braun.
Track Record
The project is intended to be the second grid-scale partnership in the collaboration. It is also the third announced commercial U.S. Xe-100 project, within an approximate 11.5 GW commercial pipeline. “At Amazon, we are committed to serving the needs of our customers and achieving our Climate Pledge goal to be net-zero carbon across our operations by 2040. This collaboration with AEP and X-energy would enable us to make progress on both while ensuring that Indiana’s communities benefit. Together, we’re looking to develop nearly a gigawatt of carbon-free power for the regional grid and pay our full costs without passing them to others. This project would also create jobs and generate tax revenues to benefit Hoosier communities for decades to come,” said Josh Weissman, VP of Data Center Infrastructure Capacity Delivery at Amazon. “This partnership brings together the experience, ambition, and innovation needed to move a project of this significance forward. AEP’s 50years of excellence in nuclear operations, combined with the world-class expertise of Amazon and technology of X-energy, are poised to chart a new course for Indiana’s energy future. Together, we’re working to advance a clean, safe, reliable solution to meet growing energy demand and benefit Indiana and its communities for generations to come,” said J. Clay Sell, CEO of X-energy.

If feasibility work supports construction, the project could move X-energy’s Xe-100 from evaluation to a commercial build in Indiana.

BETP V began its investment period in June and has already funded three platform companies: Kindle, Fisterra and Viridon. Together, these investments support new power generation capacity and electricity transmission infrastructure. The fund has also completed three acquisitions focused on energy efficiency and infrastructure resilience.
“We believe there is a generational opportunity for experienced investors in the energy transition to provide solutions to the challenges posed by growing demand for electricity. By backing exceptional management teams with flexible, patient equity capital to increase manufacturing capacity, recruit and train skilled labour and construct new critical energy infrastructure assets, BETP is delivering those solutions and in the process building these companies to scale, creating jobs and generating lasting value for our investors. We are deeply grateful for the trust of our investors and look forward to deploying BETP V in investments that advance the transition to a more affordable, reliable and cleaner energy future,” said David Foley, Global Head of Blackstone Energy Transition Partners at Blackstone.
